people.name: Gaius Licinius Stolo
people.summary: Plebeian tribune who with L. Sextius pushed through the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 on the consulship, debt and public land, after a decade of re-election.
people.detail: Livy tells that he was spurred by his wife Fabia, jealous of her sister married to a patrician consular tribune whose lictor knocked at the door. In 357 he was fined 10,000 asses under his own law for holding 1,000 iugera with his emancipated son. The cognomen Stolo ('sucker', a shoot) was explained by his care in pruning vines.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997)

people.name: Lucius Sextius Lateranus
people.summary: Colleague of Licinius in the tribunate and first plebeian consul (366).
people.detail: His consulship marks the formal admission of plebeians to supreme magistracy, though plebeian tenure was not continuous until 342.

people.name: Gaius Marcius Rutilus
people.summary: First plebeian dictator (356) and first plebeian censor (351), four times consul; the model plebeian noble of the post-367 order.
people.detail: His son C. Marcius Rutilus Censorinus, censor twice (294, 265), carried the law against iterating the censorship.

people.name: Publius Decius Mus (consul 340)
people.summary: Plebeian military tribune who saved the army at Saticula in 343 and as consul devoted himself to the gods of the underworld at the battle of Vesuvius in 340, dying to secure victory over the Latins.
people.detail: The first of three Decii credited with devotio (his son 295, grandson perhaps 279), a family tradition whose first instance may be a projection of the second.
people.death: killed charging the enemy after his devotio at the battle of Vesuvius

people.name: Publius Decius Mus (consul 295)
people.summary: Four times consul and colleague of Fabius Rullianus, who argued for the lex Ogulnia (300) and at Sentinum (295), when the Gallic chariots broke his wing, devoted himself to death in imitation of his father.
people.detail: His devotio is attested in Livy, Polybius' contemporary-era chronology and was celebrated by the dramatist Accius in a praetexta, 'Decius'.
people.death: killed after his devotio at Sentinum
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)

people.name: Quintus Publilius Philo
people.summary: Plebeian statesman of many firsts: author of the Publilian laws (339), first plebeian praetor (337), and first holder of prorogued command (proconsul at Neapolis, 326).
people.detail: Four consulships and a censorship make him one of the founders of the patricio-plebeian nobility.

people.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
people.summary: Leading patrician general of the Second Samnite War, five times consul and twice dictator, famous for his speed (Cursor), his appetite, and his severity toward his master of horse Fabius Rullianus in 325.
people.detail: Livy (9.16-19) uses him as the Roman who could have matched Alexander the Great, in a celebrated digression on what would have happened had Alexander invaded Italy. The capture of Luceria in 320 credited to him is suspect.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 184-261

people.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor (consul 293)
people.summary: Son of the dictator; won the battle of Aquilonia (293) against the Samnite linen legion, dedicated the temple of Quirinus with Rome's first sundial, and in his second consulship received the surrender of Tarentum (272).
people.detail: His Aquilonia triumph brought vast bronze and silver into the treasury; the spoils decorated the temple of Quirinus and the Forum.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus
people.summary: The dominant Roman general of the Samnite wars: five times consul, victor at Imbrinium (325), the Ciminian forest and Perusia (310) and Sentinum (295), censor who confined freedmen to the urban tribes and earned the cognomen Maximus (304).
people.detail: Defeated at Lautulae (315). Served as legate to his son Gurges in 292 and rode beside his chariot in the triumph. Great-grandfather (or grandfather) of the Cunctator. His career was surely embellished by Fabius Pictor, the first Roman historian and a member of his gens.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vols. II-IV

people.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus (consul 321)
people.summary: Consul who surrendered at the Caudine Forks in 321 and, in Livy's version, urged the Senate to repudiate the sponsio and hand him over to the Samnites, whereupon he kicked the fetial to manufacture a just cause for war.
people.detail: The cognomen Caudinus appears in some sources. The handing-over (deditio noxae) was repeated with Mancinus in Spain in 137.

people.name: Gavius Pontius
people.summary: Samnite general who trapped and humiliated the Roman army at the Caudine Forks (321); a Pontius, probably he, was captured and beheaded after the triumph of Fabius Gurges in 291.
people.detail: His father Herennius Pontius is said to have been a friend of the philosopher Archytas and to have advised either releasing the Romans with honour or killing them all. Cicero imagines Pontius wishing he had been born when Romans took bribes.
people.death: executed at Rome after Fabius Gurges' triumph (if the same man)

people.name: Appius Claudius Caecus
people.summary: Censor of 312 who built the Via Appia and Aqua Appia, reformed Senate and tribe lists in favour of freedmen's sons and the landless, and in blind old age rallied the Senate against making peace with Pyrrhus; the first Roman author known by name.
people.detail: He wrote a collection of moral sayings in Saturnian verse ('faber est suae quisque fortunae', each man is the architect of his own fortune), a speech against Pyrrhus that Cicero read, and supposedly a treatise on legal actions; he is credited with orthographic reform (replacing intervocalic s with r, e.g. Valesius to Valerius). His elogium (ILS 54) lists three interreges, two praetorships, two consulships, a dictatorship and the censorship, and the vow of the temple of Bellona.
people.death: natural causes in old age, blind
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005)

people.name: Gnaeus Flavius
people.summary: Son of a freedman and secretary to Appius Claudius who published the forms of legal action and the court calendar (304) and, to the nobility's fury, was elected curule aedile.
people.detail: He dedicated a bronze shrine to Concord in the Graecostasis, vowed without the Senate's approval; the episode produced a law requiring Senate or tribune consent for dedications. Livy draws on the annalist Licinius Macer and on Piso for his story.

people.name: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus
people.summary: Plebeian tribune who with his brother Gnaeus carried the lex Ogulnia (300) opening the priesthoods; as aedile set up the she-wolf and twins at the Ficus Ruminalis (296); led the embassy that brought Aesculapius to Rome and the embassy to Ptolemy II; consul 269.
people.detail: A neat example of a plebeian noble whose career spans religious reform, monument-building and Hellenistic diplomacy in the generation before the Punic Wars.

people.name: Gellius Egnatius
people.summary: Samnite general who led an army into Etruria in 296 and forged the coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls; killed at Sentinum.
people.detail: The Egnatii were a prominent Samnite family; Marius Egnatius led the Samnites in the Social War (90-89).

people.name: Scipio Barbatus
people.summary: Consul of 298, first occupant of the Tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, whose sarcophagus epitaph claims victories in Samnium (Taurasia, Cisauna) and the subjugation of Lucania, contradicting Livy's account.
people.detail: Great-grandfather of Scipio Africanus. The epitaph, in Saturnian verse, praises him as 'brave and wise, whose appearance matched his virtue'. Livy has him serve as legate at Sentinum and propraetor in 295 (the commander of the legion destroyed at Camerinum was 'L. Scipio').
scholarship: Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972)

people.name: Manius Curius Dentatus
people.summary: Plebeian 'new man' who conquered the Sabines and Praetuttii (290), defeated Pyrrhus at Beneventum (275), drained the Lacus Velinus and as censor began the Anio Vetus aqueduct; the paragon of rustic incorruptibility.
people.detail: Samnite envoys found him roasting turnips at his hearth and were told he preferred ruling those who had gold to having it. He won two triumphs (Samnites and Sabines in 290, Pyrrhus in 275) and an ovation over the Lucanians. Cato the Elder admired his farmhouse near Reate.
people.death: died in office as a commissioner for the Anio Vetus
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 334-335

people.name: Quintus Hortensius
people.summary: Plebeian dictator appointed during the last secession of the plebs (to the Janiculum) who carried the lex Hortensia making plebiscites binding on all citizens; he died in office.
people.detail: Almost nothing else is known; the relevant books of Livy are lost.

people.name: Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter
people.summary: First consul of the plebeian Caecilii Metelli (284), killed with much of his army when relieving Arretium from the Senones.
people.detail: Polybius calls the Roman commander a praetor; Livy's epitome and Orosius report 13,000 dead. The Metelli became one of the most powerful families of the later Republic.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella (consul 283)
people.summary: Consul who destroyed the Boii and Etruscans at Lake Vadimon (283) and helped clear the Senones from the ager Gallicus.
people.detail: Ancestor of the later Cornelii Dolabellae, including Cicero's son-in-law.

people.name: Lucius Postumius Megellus
people.summary: Three times consul, victor at Bovianum (305), dedicator of the temple of Victoria (294), and the envoy whose toga was soiled by a Tarentine in 282, promising that the stain would be washed out with blood.
people.detail: Known for arrogance: he triumphed in 294 without Senate approval and in 291 used 2,000 soldiers to clear woodland on his estate, for which he was fined.

people.name: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
people.summary: New man from Aletrium who relieved Thurii (282), negotiated with Pyrrhus over prisoners refusing his gifts, returned the king's would-be poisoner (278) and as censor expelled P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.
people.detail: With Curius Dentatus he became the late Republic's emblem of poor but incorruptible early Romans (Cicero, Virgil 'parvoque potentem Fabricium'). He was so poor that the state provided his daughters' dowries.

people.name: Publius Valerius Laevinus
people.summary: Consul defeated by Pyrrhus at Heraclea (280) when the elephants routed his cavalry; he regrouped and shadowed Pyrrhus' march on Rome.
people.detail: Plutarch reports that he refused Pyrrhus' offer of arbitration, saying the Romans neither accepted him as judge nor feared him as enemy.

people.name: Tiberius Coruncanius
people.summary: New man from Tusculum, consul in 280 who triumphed over Vulsinii and Vulci and shielded Rome against Pyrrhus' advance; the first plebeian pontifex maximus and the first to give public instruction in law.
people.detail: Pomponius' history of jurisprudence (Digest 1.2.2.35, 38) names him as the first to profess law publicly, building on Flavius' publication. No writings survived.

people.name: Cineas
people.summary: Thessalian orator, reputedly a pupil of Demosthenes, who served Pyrrhus as diplomat; Pyrrhus said Cineas had won more cities by words than he by arms. He led the 280/279 peace embassy to Rome.
people.detail: He reportedly learned the names of Roman senators and equites within a day of arriving. He epitomised Aeneas Tacticus' work on siegecraft. Plutarch's dialogue in which he asks Pyrrhus what he will do after conquering Italy, Sicily and Carthage is the classic critique of limitless ambition.

people.name: Pyrrhus
people.fullName: Pyrrhus son of Aeacides, king of the Molossians and Epirus
people.summary: Hellenistic king of Epirus, kinsman of Alexander the Great, who answered Tarentum's call in 280, defeated Rome at Heraclea and Ausculum, conquered most of Carthaginian Sicily, and after the check at Beneventum (275) returned to Greece, dying in street fighting at Argos.
people.detail: A hostage at Ptolemy I's court, he married Ptolemy's stepdaughter Antigone and later Agathocles' daughter Lanassa. He wrote a manual on tactics and memoirs; Hannibal rated him among the greatest generals. His Italian war established Rome's reputation in the Greek world (Ptolemy II's embassy, 273) and gave Rome its first experience of a professional Hellenistic army and elephants.
people.death: stunned by a roof tile thrown by an old woman at Argos and beheaded by a soldier of Antigonus Gonatas
scholarship: Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

people.name: Gelon
people.summary: Deinomenid tyrant of Gela and then Syracuse, which he made the greatest Greek city of the west by mass transfers of population; victor over Carthage at Himera (480).
people.detail: He offered the mainland Greeks 200 triremes and 28,000 men against Xerxes on condition of command (Herodotus). Dionysius of Halicarnassus' story that he sent grain to Rome in 492 is an anachronism criticised by Dionysius himself.

people.name: Hiero I
people.summary: Brother and successor of Gelon who crushed the Etruscan fleet off Cumae (474) and was patron of Pindar, Bacchylides, Simonides and Aeschylus.
people.detail: His dedicated Etruscan helmets from the Cumae spoils survive from Olympia. He founded Aetna (Catana) for his son.

people.name: Dionysius I
people.summary: Tyrant of Syracuse for 38 years who fought four wars with Carthage (destroying Motya in 397), crushed the Italiote League at the Elleporus (389), took Rhegium (387), raided Pyrgi (384) and founded Adriatic outposts.
people.detail: He pioneered artillery, quinqueremes and great siege trains; wrote tragedies (one won at the Lenaea in 367); employed Celtic and Iberian mercenaries and allied with the Gauls who had sacked Rome (Justin 20.5). Plato's visits to Syracuse involved his son and successor.
people.death: natural causes (allegedly hastened by his physicians)
scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I: War-Lord of Sicily (1990)

people.name: Timoleon
people.fullName: Timoleon son of Timodemus of Corinth
people.summary: Corinthian liberator who expelled Dionysius II and other Sicilian tyrants, defeated Carthage at the Crimissus (341 or 339) and resettled Greek Sicily with thousands of colonists before retiring.
people.detail: Plutarch paired him with Aemilius Paullus. He went blind in his last years and was buried at public expense in Syracuse, with a gymnasium called the Timoleonteum.
scholarship: Talbert, Timoleon and the Revival of Greek Sicily (1974)

people.name: Alexander of Epirus
people.fullName: Alexander I son of Neoptolemus, king of the Molossians
people.summary: Brother of Olympias and uncle and brother-in-law of Alexander the Great, who campaigned in southern Italy for Tarentum (334-331), made a treaty with Rome, and was killed at Pandosia in Bruttium.
people.detail: Livy (8.24) and Justin report his saying that his nephew had fought women in Asia while he fought men in Italy. Installed by Philip II, he married Philip's daughter Cleopatra in 336 at the wedding where Philip was murdered.
people.death: killed crossing the Acheron at Pandosia

people.name: Archytas of Tarentum
people.summary: Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician and statesman who led Tarentum, head of the Italiote League, at the height of its power, and rescued Plato from Dionysius II in 361.
people.detail: He solved the problem of doubling the cube, worked on harmonics and mechanics (a flying wooden dove is attributed to him), and was elected general seven years running despite a legal limit, never defeated. Cicero has the Samnite Herennius Pontius converse with him.
people.death: drowned or shipwrecked off Apulia (Horace, Odes 1.28)

people.name: Agathocles
people.summary: Potter's son turned tyrant of Syracuse who invaded Carthaginian Africa (310-307), took the royal title (304), intervened in southern Italy against the Bruttians and seized Corcyra, and married his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus.
people.detail: His Campanian mercenaries, discharged at his death, became the Mamertines who seized Messana. Polybius cited Scipio Africanus' admiration for Agathocles and Dionysius as men who combined daring with intelligence. He renounced restoring Syracusan democracy on his deathbed (Diodorus).

people.name: Cleonymus of Sparta
people.summary: Spartan prince, passed over for the throne, who was hired by Tarentum against the Lucanians and Romans (303-302) and after setbacks raided the Adriatic coast until defeated by the Patavini.
people.detail: He later invited Pyrrhus to attack Sparta in 272, a campaign that preceded Pyrrhus' death at Argos.

people.name: Hiero II
people.summary: Syracusan officer of Pyrrhus' army who became general, defeated the Mamertines at the Longanus and was acclaimed king; he assisted Rome at Rhegium (270), fought Rome briefly in 264-263, and then reigned for half a century as Rome's most loyal ally.
people.detail: Polybius praises his moderation. His tax law (lex Hieronica) was adopted by Rome for Sicily. Patron of Archimedes, and builder of the giant ship Syracusia and the great altar of Syracuse.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 54-56
